title: Connected bodies & pulleys
examples: How do I find the tension in a pulley system?
What is the relationship between tension and acceleration?
Can you explain how to calculate the acceleration of two connected masses?

explain.say: Today we will look at connected bodies using pulleys. We will learn about tension in the string.

items: string: The force pulling the masses

explain.say: Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: pulleys. Look at the fixed pulley, the movable pulley and the rope. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
Tension is the pulling force transmitted through a string. It pulls on both connected objects.
When bodies are connected, they share the same acceleration. This is a key idea to remember.
We use Newton's second law for each body separately. This helps us find the unknown tension.
Consider two masses hanging over a pulley. The tension pulls up on both masses.
In real life, think about lifting a heavy box with a pulley. The tension supports the weight of the box.

faq.q: Do the connected masses always accelerate together?
faq.a: Yes, if they are connected by a string over a pulley, they must share the same magnitude of acceleration. This is because the string cannot stretch.
asks: Must the acceleration be the same?
If they are connected, do they move together?

faq.q: How do I choose which equation to use for tension?
faq.a: You must apply Newton's second law to each object individually. Remember to account for the direction of motion when setting up your forces.
asks: Should I use the same equation for both sides?
Does the tension equation change based on the pulley?

faq.q: Is the tension always equal to the weight of the object?
faq.a: No, tension is only equal to the weight if the object is not accelerating. If it is accelerating, the tension will be different from the weight.
asks: Can tension be different from the weight?

faq.q: What if the pulley itself has mass?
faq.a: If the pulley has mass, you must include the rotational inertia of the pulley in your calculations. This makes the system more complex.
asks: Do I worry about the pulley's mass?
How does pulley mass affect acceleration?

faq.q: Does the direction of acceleration matter for the tension?
faq.a: The direction determines the sign in your force equations. If the object accelerates down, the net force calculation reflects that direction.
asks: Does direction matter in the math?
How do I set up forces for downward motion?

facts: Tension is a pulling force transmitted through a string or cable.
For connected bodies, the acceleration magnitude is the same for all parts.
Newton's second law, F equals mass times acceleration, applies to each body.
When calculating tension, the direction of motion determines the sign in the force equation.

quiz.say: Two masses, one of 10 kilograms and one of 5 kilograms, are connected over a pulley. If the total acceleration is 1 meter per second squared, what is the tension in the string?
quiz.why: You must sum the forces correctly: T - 50 N = 5 1, and T - 100 N = 10 1, which gives T = 12.5 N.

wrong.0: This incorrectly sets the tension equal to the weight of the smaller mass.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes the tension is half the total weight.
wrong.3: This only calculates the weight of the larger mass, ignoring the smaller mass's effect.

quiz.say: A 20 kilogram block is pulled by a string over a pulley. If the tension is 80 Newtons, what is the block's acceleration?
quiz.why: Use the equation Fnet = T - mg. So, 80 N - (20 kg 9.8 m/s²) = 20 kg a. This gives a = 2 m/s².

wrong.1: This assumes the tension equals the weight, which is only true if there is no acceleration.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the tension value as the net force.
wrong.3: This uses an incorrect value for the net force calculation.

quiz.say: If two masses are connected and accelerating, which physical quantity must be the same for both masses?
quiz.why: Because they are connected by a single string, the rate of change of position, or acceleration, must be identical for both masses.

wrong.0: The net force is different because the masses are different.
wrong.1: The weight depends on the mass, so it will be different for different masses.
wrong.3: Tension is the same, but the acceleration is what must be equal for both bodies.
